\phantomsection\section*{Abstract}\label{sec:abstract}\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Abstract}

This thesis asks whether water and sanitation (WASH) conditions are associated with the anthropometric outcomes of children under five --- height-for-age (HAZ), weight-for-age (WAZ) and weight-for-height (WHZ) z-scores --- in four Sub-Saharan African countries: Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria, selected for data availability and recency, not to represent the region as a whole. The baseline analysis distinguishes a child's own household facilities from the WASH conditions of the surrounding community. Both analyses are cross-sectional and observational; every estimate is reported as an association, not a causal effect.

The baseline sample pools the most recent Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) round for each country (2022--2025). Household WASH is the improved/unimproved facility classification of the child's own household; community WASH is a leave-one-out rate of improved-facility coverage among other sampled households in the same DHS cluster, excluding the child's own household. Each exposure is estimated under the fixed-effects structure its construction requires: cluster fixed effects for household WASH, region fixed effects for community WASH, which varies almost only between clusters. No household cluster-fixed-effects coefficient reaches significance at the 5\% level for any outcome (water--HAZ comes closest, \emph{p} = .062); these results are inconclusive rather than evidence that no association exists. Community coverage shows a large, significant association before covariate adjustment for most outcome--exposure pairs, which attenuates to non-significance once socioeconomic controls and region fixed effects are added --- consistent with, but not proof of, confounding by local socioeconomic conditions.

A separate, preliminary extension uses an independently constructed sample --- earlier DHS rounds for Ghana (2014), Kenya (2014) and Nigeria (2018), harmonised by IPUMS-DHS and linked to modelled annual gridded WASH coverage from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) --- to address one limitation of the baseline design, which records WASH once, at the survey date, rather than during each child's own early life. It asks whether modelled coverage during a child's first 12 postnatal months is associated with later outcomes, using cluster fixed effects and country-specific birth-year terms; Ethiopia enters only as a provisional sensitivity analysis, since its interview-date conversion could not be validated. The exposure is an area average of modelled coverage around displaced cluster coordinates, neither observed household access nor population-weighted coverage, and the historical data cannot separate a child's household from its community.

The selected primary finding is the pooled established-date association between local water coverage and HAZ: β = 1.03 per 10 percentage points (95\% CI {[}0.51, 1.54{]}, \emph{p} \textless{} .001) --- one of six nominally significant cells among 24 primary cells, with no multiple-testing adjustment applied, and sensitive to the pooled weighting convention (0.41, \emph{p} = .035, unweighted on the same observations). All 24 primary cells were reproduced with a second estimation library on a separately rebuilt sample, confirming the computation, not causality. The estimates are weighted conditional associations among eligible measured children --- no official documentation of an anthropometry-specific sampling weight could be located --- and the exposure source draws partly on the same DHS surveys it is compared against.

Because the baseline and historical samples differ at once in children, survey rounds, exposure construction, eligibility rules and control sets, the contrast between the largely null baseline results and the historical finding cannot be attributed to exposure timing; the historical result is preliminary and does not overturn the baseline conclusions. The thesis contributes a side-by-side household/community WASH comparison within one four-country sample, and a preliminary extension assigning modelled local coverage to each child's early-life window, each read with its own limitations. None of the results bears on the effectiveness of WASH investment as a policy instrument.
